course.title: Advanced Artificial Intelligence
course.description: From core concepts of modern AI and generative models to practical tool use and advanced prompting. Progressive path from curious beginner to confident advanced user.

modules.title: Module 1: Modern AI technologies
modules.description: How AI and machine learning work at a conceptual level.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: How AI and machine learning work
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Explain in plain language what machine learning does and how it differs from traditional programming.

Key ideas

Traditional software follows explicit rules written by people. Machine learning systems learn patterns from examples. Training uses data; inference applies the learned pattern to new cases. Limitations include data bias, brittleness outside the training distribution, and lack of true understanding.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Key AI technologies today
lessons.description: Vision, language, speech, recommendation and more.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Name major AI application areas and give a realistic example of each.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Opportunities and limitations
lessons.description: Where AI helps and where it fails.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

List practical opportunities and important limitations of current AI systems.

lessons.title: Module 1 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 1 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Machine learning primarily learns from:
Only hand-written rules
*Examples / data
Random numbers only
User passwords
explain: Learning from data is the core idea.
level: 1

Q: A key limitation of current AI is:
It never makes mistakes
*It can fail on cases unlike its training data
It requires no data
It always explains its reasoning perfectly
explain: Distribution shift causes failures.
level: 2

Q: Traditional programming differs from ML because:
It never uses data
*It relies on explicit rules written by developers
It cannot run on computers
It is identical to ML
explain: Explicit rules vs learned patterns.
level: 1

Q: Bias in training data can lead to:
Perfect fairness always
*Biased or unfair model behaviour
Faster training only
No effect
explain: Models reflect their data.
level: 1

Q: Computer vision systems mainly process:
Only text
*Images and video
Only audio
Only spreadsheets
explain: Vision = visual input.
level: 1

Q: Recommendation systems typically:
Ignore user behaviour
*Suggest items based on patterns in past behaviour and content
Only work offline
Replace all search
explain: Patterns drive recommendations.
level: 2

Q: “AI understands language like humans” is:
Strictly true for all systems
*An overstatement; systems predict and pattern-match without human-like understanding
Required by law
Only true for images
explain: Current systems lack human understanding.
level: 2

Q: A practical opportunity for AI is:
Eliminating all human judgement forever
*Automating repetitive pattern-based tasks and augmenting human work
Removing the need for data
Guaranteeing zero errors
explain: Augmentation and automation of suitable tasks.
level: 1

Q: Evaluating an AI system should include:
Only marketing claims
*Testing on realistic data and monitoring real-world performance
Ignoring failures
Using only training data for evaluation
explain: Realistic evaluation is essential.
level: 2

Q: The difference between training and inference is:
There is no difference
*Training learns from data; inference applies the learned model to new inputs
Inference happens only once ever
Training requires no data
explain: Two distinct phases.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 2: Generative AI and large language models
modules.description: How generative models create content and where they go wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: How generative AI creates content
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Explain at a high level how large language models generate text.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Inside large language models
lessons.description: Scale, training data and emergent abilities.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Describe why scale and diverse training data matter, and what “emergent” abilities roughly means.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Strengths, errors and hallucinations
lessons.description: When to trust and when to verify.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Recognise strengths of LLMs and the reality of hallucinations; adopt a verify-important-claims habit.

lessons.title: Module 2 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 2 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Large language models generate text largely by:
Looking up exact documents only
*Predicting likely next tokens given context
Running SQL queries
Random character selection only
explain: Next-token prediction is central.
level: 1

Q: A hallucination in this context is:
A perfect citation
*A fluent but incorrect or fabricated statement
A type of image
A security feature
explain: Fluent falsehoods are a known risk.
level: 1

Q: Important factual claims from an LLM should be:
Always trusted blindly
*Verified against reliable sources when decisions matter
Ignored completely
Only used for poetry
explain: Verification protects decisions.
level: 1

Q: Scale of models and data often:
Has no effect
*Improves capability on many tasks, with diminishing and uneven returns
Guarantees zero errors
Removes the need for prompts
explain: Scale helps but is not magic.
level: 2

Q: Generative AI is strong at:
Guaranteeing legal advice
*Drafting, summarising, brainstorming and transforming text when guided well
Replacing all databases
Never needing human review
explain: Strong at language tasks under guidance.
level: 1

Q: Training data influences:
Only the model’s colour scheme
*What the model can do well and where it may be biased or outdated
Only inference speed
Nothing
explain: Data shapes behaviour.
level: 2

Q: “Emergent abilities” roughly refers to:
Abilities that appear only after certain scale thresholds
*Capabilities that become apparent at larger scales and were not explicitly programmed as narrow rules
Only image generation
Hardware failures
explain: Scale can unlock new behaviours.
level: 2

Q: Using an LLM for medical or legal decisions without expert review is:
Always safe
*Risky because of errors and lack of accountability
Required
The only modern approach
explain: High-stakes domains need expertise.
level: 1

Q: Temperature (sampling) settings affect:
Database schema
*How random or focused the generated text is
Only image resolution
User passwords
explain: Sampling controls variability.
level: 2

Q: A practical habit with generative AI is:
Never read the output
*Treat it as a draft that needs human judgement and verification for important uses
Publish every output immediately
Avoid all creativity
explain: Human-in-the-loop is wise.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 3: AI tools
modules.description: Choose and use text, image and productivity tools responsibly.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Choosing the right AI tool
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Select an appropriate tool category for a given task and recognise when AI is not the best approach.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Text, image and productivity tools
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply common tools to drafting, summarising, image generation and workflow support.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.3: Using tools safely and responsibly
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply basic rules for sensitive data, copyright and organisational policy when using AI tools.

lessons.title: Module 3 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 3 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The first step in choosing an AI tool is:
Picking the most expensive option
*Clarifying the task and constraints (privacy, accuracy needs, budget)
Ignoring the task
Using every tool at once
explain: Task clarity guides selection.
level: 1

Q: Pasting confidential customer data into a public AI tool is:
Always fine
*A privacy and policy risk
Required for good results
Only a problem for images
explain: Sensitive data needs protection.
level: 1

Q: AI image generators may raise:
No issues ever
*Copyright, likeness and misuse concerns
Only colour problems
Only speed issues
explain: Legal and ethical issues exist.
level: 2

Q: Workplace AI use should follow:
Only personal preference
*Organisational policy and applicable law
No rules
Only the tool’s marketing page
explain: Policy and law apply.
level: 1

Q: AI is often a poor fit when:
The task is repetitive pattern matching
*The cost of errors is extreme and no reliable verification exists
You need a first draft
You want brainstorming help
explain: High-stakes unverified use is dangerous.
level: 2

Q: Summarising a long document with AI is useful when:
You never check the summary
*You still verify key points for important decisions
The document is secret and the tool is public
You delete the original forever
explain: Verification remains necessary.
level: 1

Q: Productivity AI tools can help with:
Only replacing all staff
*Drafting, scheduling support, email cleanup and similar tasks under human oversight
Guaranteeing zero mistakes
Avoiding all learning
explain: Augmentation under oversight.
level: 1

Q: Attribution and originality concerns arise especially with:
Simple calculators
*Generated text and images that may closely resemble existing works
Spreadsheets only
Hardware
explain: Generative outputs can raise IP issues.
level: 2

Q: A responsible default is:
Share all company data with every tool
*Minimise sensitive data shared with external tools
Ignore all policies
Use the same password everywhere
explain: Data minimisation is prudent.
level: 1

Q: When AI output will be published under your name you should:
Never read it
*Review and edit so you stand behind the final version
Copy it unchanged always
Hide the use of AI in all cases without considering policy
explain: You remain accountable.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 4: Advanced prompting
modules.description: Engineer prompts that reliably produce useful results.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Prompt engineering principles
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Write prompts that specify role, task, context, format and constraints clearly.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Structuring complex prompts
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Break complex tasks into steps and use examples (few-shot) when helpful.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.3: Testing and improving prompts
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Define what “good” looks like and iterate prompts against that standard.

lessons.title: Module 4 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 4 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: A strong prompt usually includes:
Only one vague word
*Clear task, relevant context, desired format and constraints
Only the model’s name
Random characters
explain: Specificity improves results.
level: 1

Q: Assigning a role in a prompt can:
Never help
*Focus the style and expertise the model tries to emulate
Delete the model
Change the weather
explain: Role-setting shapes output.
level: 1

Q: Few-shot prompting means:
Using no examples
*Providing a few input-output examples in the prompt
Training a new model from scratch
Only using images
explain: Examples guide the pattern.
level: 1

Q: For complex tasks it often helps to:
Ask for everything in one vague sentence
*Break the work into ordered steps
Avoid all structure
Use only one-word prompts
explain: Decomposition improves reliability.
level: 1

Q: Evaluating prompt quality requires:
Only liking the first output
*Criteria for what “good enough” means and iterative testing
Never changing the prompt
Ignoring failures
explain: Criteria + iteration = improvement.
level: 2

Q: Specifying output format (e.g. bullet list, JSON, table) helps because:
Models ignore format
*It makes results easier to use and compare
It always reduces accuracy
It is only for images
explain: Format constraints aid usability.
level: 1

Q: Adding irrelevant context to a prompt usually:
Improves focus
*Dilutes attention and can hurt results
Is required
Only affects colour
explain: Relevant context is better.
level: 2

Q: When a prompt fails you should:
Give up permanently
*Diagnose (ambiguity, missing context, wrong constraints) and revise
Only buy a new computer
Blame the user of the output
explain: Systematic revision works.
level: 1

Q: Constraints such as “use only the provided text” help:
Encourage hallucination
*Reduce fabrication and keep answers grounded
Slow the model only
Hide all sources
explain: Grounding constraints reduce hallucinations.
level: 2

Q: Advanced prompting is best viewed as:
A one-time magic spell
*An iterative engineering skill that improves with practice and evaluation
Unnecessary for all tasks
Only for researchers
explain: Skill + iteration beats one-shot luck.
level: 1
